analysis.one_liner: Ends billions of dollars in federal subsidies, tax breaks, and liability limits for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to seven House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shut down the special tax breaks and subsidies the federal government gives to oil, gas, and coal companies. It would end deductions and credits unique to drilling and mining, raise the royalty rate companies pay for extracting oil, gas, and coal from federal lands from 12.5% to 18.75%, stop federal agencies and export-credit banks from financing fossil fuel projects, and remove the cap on what companies must pay when they cause an oil spill. It would also impose a 13% tax on oil and gas taken from the Gulf of Mexico's outer continental shelf.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently make up the difference when oil and gas companies pay reduced royalties on federal land, deduct drilling costs immediately, and cap their spill liability. If the bill passed, the public would collect more from federal energy leases, and the revenue from closing these tax breaks could reduce deficits or fund other priorities. Communities affected by spills and mining would gain from unlimited company liability and a permanently funded Black Lung Disability Trust Fund.

how_it_helps.text: It terminates dozens of special tax breaks for oil, gas, and coal companies, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion, last-in-first-out accounting, and special treatment of intangible drilling costs—closing preferences other industries do not get.
It raises the royalty rate companies pay for oil, gas, and coal taken from federal lands from 12.5% to 18.75%, so taxpayers get a bigger share of the value of publicly owned resources.
It ends royalty relief and caps on what offshore drillers and pipeline operators must pay when they cause a spill, meaning taxpayers are less likely to be stuck with cleanup costs.
It bars federal agencies and export-credit agencies from financing fossil fuel projects abroad, and it stops the Department of Energy's dedicated fossil fuel research program.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies would lose the deductions, credits, royalty relief, and liability caps the bill repeals, and would pay the new excise taxes. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through higher fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: The new 13% excise tax on Gulf of Mexico oil and gas production and the increased oil-spill financing rate would raise production costs that companies could pass on to consumers through higher fuel and energy prices.

The bill repeals the carbon oxide sequestration tax credit (45Q), a tool some climate advocates support for keeping carbon captured from industrial sources underground, and ends the refined-coal production credit.

Extending amortization periods and ending immediate expensing for drilling and mining costs raises the cost of capital for an industry that still supplies most of the country's energy, which critics argue could slow domestic production and increase reliance on imports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—ending billions of dollars in tax preferences, fee holidays, and government-backed financing for fossil fuel companies—would come at the cost of somewhat higher energy prices and steeper taxes on fossil fuel firms, which are significant. The subsidy provisions do nothing to raise money directly for public services; they simply stop preferential treatment, which makes them easy to defend. The removal of the 45Q carbon-capture credit is the most debatable piece, since that credit has some support among climate advocates as a decarbonization tool. On balance the bill's benefits to taxpayers and public revenue outweigh its costs, but it was never seriously weighed because it never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to seven House committees at introduction, none of which acted on it, and it sat there until the congressional session ended with no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act on March 19, 2021; it was referred to seven committees—Ways and Means, Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, Financial Services, Science, Space, and Technology, Agriculture, and Energy and Commerce.
Its only further action was referral to three subcommittees between March and May 2021; no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in its action history.
All 47 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on.
The bill never advanced and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which keep the federal subsidies, tax preferences, and liability limits the bill would have ended. Taxpayers continue covering the difference.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies keeping their subsidies

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 47 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's cosponsors was a Republican, leaving it without the minority support that would have pressured leadership to act.

sides.party_line_note: All 47 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported the bill, so the fight followed party lines even though it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would end dozens of tax preferences (intangible drilling cost expensing, percentage depletion, enhanced oil recovery credits), raise federal royalty rates from 12.5% to 18.75%, and expose companies to unlimited spill liability. Its death preserved those subsidies.

The bill repeals percentage depletion and capital gains treatment for coal royalties, raises the excise tax funding the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, and studies higher royalties in the Powder River Basin. Its death left these benefits intact.

The bill would remove liability caps for offshore facilities and pipeline operators and deny tax deductions for oil spill cleanup costs. The companies' gain from its failure is the public's continued exposure to cleanup costs.

industries.industry: Export-credit and international finance institutions (Export-Import Bank, DFC)
industries.note: The bill would bar these agencies from financing overseas fossil fuel projects; the prohibition never took effect, so the agencies continue backing fossil fuel transactions abroad.
